sunday.themeNote: All three readings this week point to the same surprising truth: God's love and welcome reach much further than we might expect. Isaiah says God's house is a place of prayer for all peoples, not just a chosen few. Paul explains that mercy flows outward to everyone, even those who feel far from God. And in the Gospel, a woman who is a complete outsider receives one of the greatest compliments Jesus ever gives anyone.

readings.label: First Reading
readings.fullText:
Thus says the LORD:
Observe what is right, do what is just;
for my salvation is about to come,
my justice, about to be revealed.

The foreigners who join themselves to the LORD,
ministering to him,
loving the name of the LORD,
and becoming his servants—
all who keep the sabbath free from profanation
and hold to my covenant,
them I will bring to my holy mountain
and make joyful in my house of prayer;
their burnt offerings and sacrifices
will be acceptable on my altar,
for my house shall be called
a house of prayer for all peoples.
readings.summary: God speaks through the prophet Isaiah and says that anyone who loves him and tries to do what is right belongs at his holy mountain. This includes people who were not born into the Israelite community. God promises to welcome them, hear their prayers, and accept their worship. His house, God says, is a house of prayer for all peoples.

reflection.reflection: God is not looking for perfect people or insiders. He is looking for anyone who tries to do right and wants to be close to him.
reflection.question: Is there a moment this week when you felt like you didn't quite belong somewhere? What would it feel like to know you had a guaranteed seat at the table?

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.fullText:
R. (4) O God, let all the nations praise you!
May God have pity on us and bless us;
may he let his face shine upon us.
So may your way be known upon earth;
among all nations, your salvation.
R. O God, let all the nations praise you!
May the nations be glad and exult
because you rule the peoples in equity;
the nations on the earth you guide.
R. O God, let all the nations praise you!
May the peoples praise you, O God;
may all the peoples praise you!
May God bless us,
and may all the ends of the earth fear him!
R. O God, let all the nations praise you!
readings.summary: This psalm is a joyful prayer asking God to bless everyone on earth and to let all nations know his goodness. The people pray that God's ways would be seen and known across the whole world. Every nation is invited to praise him together. The refrain celebrates a God who guides all people with fairness.

reflection.reflection: God's goodness is not meant to stay with one group of people. It is meant to spill outward until everyone has a chance to experience it.
reflection.question: Think of one person in your life who seems unlikely to be on your side. What would it look like to genuinely hope good things for them this week?

readings.label: Second Reading
readings.fullText:
Brothers and sisters:
I am speaking to you Gentiles.
Inasmuch as I am the apostle to the Gentiles,
I glory in my ministry in order to make my race jealous
and thus save some of them.
For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world,
what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?

For the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable.
Just as you once disobeyed God
but have now received mercy because of their disobedience,
so they have now disobeyed in order that,
by virtue of the mercy shown to you,
they too may now receive mercy.
For God delivered all to disobedience,
that he might have mercy upon all.
readings.summary: Paul is writing to non-Jewish Christians in Rome, reminding them that God's mercy is not a limited resource. He explains that God allowed both Jewish and non-Jewish people to stumble so that he could show mercy to both. No gift or promise God makes is ever taken back. In the end, Paul says, God's plan has always been to show mercy to everyone.

reflection.reflection: Mercy is not something God runs out of. No matter how far someone has drifted, they are still within reach of it.
reflection.question: Is there something you have done or left undone that makes you feel like you are too far gone to be welcomed back? What would it mean if that feeling simply wasn't true?

readings.label: Gospel
readings.fullText:
At that time, Jesus withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon.
And behold, a Canaanite woman of that district came and called out,
"Have pity on me, Lord, Son of David!
My daughter is tormented by a demon."
But Jesus did not say a word in answer to her.
Jesus' disciples came and asked him,
"Send her away, for she keeps calling out after us."
He said in reply,
"I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."
But the woman came and did Jesus homage, saying, "Lord, help me."
He said in reply,
"It is not right to take the food of the children
and throw it to the dogs."
She said, "Please, Lord, for even the dogs eat the scraps
that fall from the table of their masters."
Then Jesus said to her in reply,
"O woman, great is your faith!
Let it be done for you as you wish."
And the woman's daughter was healed from that hour.
readings.summary: A woman from outside the Jewish community approaches Jesus, begging him to heal her daughter. At first Jesus does not respond, and his disciples want to send her away. But the woman keeps asking, and when Jesus tests her with a hard reply, she answers with humble, quick-witted trust. Jesus is moved and praises her faith, and her daughter is healed immediately.

reflection.reflection: The woman in this story did not give up or back down, even when it looked like the answer was no. Her honesty and persistence were exactly what opened the door.
reflection.question: When something matters deeply to you and the answer keeps seeming like a no, what usually happens to your patience? What helps you keep showing up anyway?
